one_line_idea: Same-tile multi-temporal imagery isolates the sun-geometry shortcut in optical remote sensing: land-cover predictions flip with sun elevation on unchanged scenes, quantifying a shadow-driven confound that scene-level models silently exploit.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Optical satellite scenes carry acquisition-time shadow structure set by sun elevation and azimuth, which co-varies with season and latitude; models trained across regions therefore see sun geometry correlated with land-cover priors.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A measurable fraction of land-cover classification variance on physically unchanged tiles is attributable to sun geometry alone: evaluating fixed tiles imaged at many sun angles (repeat acquisitions, no land change) will show prediction instability that correlates with shadow-fraction change, and shadow-normalized inputs will reduce it.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On verified-unchanged tile pairs spanning large sun-elevation differences, at least 8% of pixels/patches will flip predicted class, flips will correlate with local shadow-fraction change (r >= 0.4), and shadow-aware normalization will cut flips by at least 30%; kill the idea if flip rate is under 2% or uncorrelated with shadow change.
why_important: Change detection and monitoring systems interpret prediction flips as land change; a quantified sun-geometry flip rate sets the noise floor and offers an immediate correction lever.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Illumination effects are folklore in remote sensing; a controlled same-tile quantification against modern models with a normalization intervention appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select multi-temporal same-tile stacks with metadata-verified stability, run fixed classifiers across acquisitions, regress prediction flips on sun-geometry deltas and shadow-fraction changes, and evaluate the normalization variant.
main_risk: Verifying 'no land change' requires care (agriculture changes rapidly); the design must use stable land covers like dense forest interior and urban cores.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Sun geometry is assumed absorbed by data diversity and augmentation, with residual effects considered negligible.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Radiometric preprocessing may already remove most sun-elevation signal, making residual flips small.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: fMoW multi-temporal imagery (timestamps and metadata public) with its public ResNet baseline or SatMAE; the analysis runs in about 10 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$20).

one_line_idea: Off-nadir viewing angle degrades building extraction through two separable mechanisms (facade visibility and resolution anisotropy), and an angle-conditioned model that reasons about facade displacement beats angle-agnostic training on high-off-nadir imagery.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Satellite images are frequently collected off-nadir (especially in rapid-response tasking), where buildings show facades and displaced roofs; public benchmarks demonstrate large accuracy drops at high angles, but the mechanism mix is unquantified.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The off-nadir drop decomposes into (a) geometric displacement between roof and footprint, correctable with angle metadata, and (b) genuine information loss from resolution anisotropy and occlusion; an angle-conditioned model with an explicit roof-to-footprint offset head will recover most of component (a), and the residual curve versus angle will quantify component (b) as the true physical limit.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The offset-head model will recover at least 50% of the footprint-extraction F1 drop at 40-50 degree off-nadir angles relative to nadir-trained baselines; kill the idea if recovery is under 20%, implying the drop is mostly irreversible information loss rather than correctable geometry.
why_important: Disaster mapping uses whatever geometry is available fastest, which is usually off-nadir; separating correctable from physical loss tells responders what accuracy to expect and vendors what to fix.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Off-nadir challenges established the drop exists; the two-mechanism decomposition with an offset-head recovery fraction appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train baseline and angle-conditioned offset-head models on a public multi-angle building dataset, evaluate F1 versus angle, and attribute recovered versus residual components.
main_risk: Angle is confounded with atmospheric path length and sun geometry in real collects; the dataset's angle diversity must be checked for such couplings.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Off-nadir robustness is pursued with data augmentation and more high-angle training data, treating the drop as generic domain shift.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Roof-footprint displacement may already be learned implicitly by segmentation heads given enough high-angle training data, leaving little for the explicit head.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: SpaceNet 4 (multi-off-nadir Atlanta collects) with U-Net/HRNet baselines; training and the angle sweep run in about 30 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$60).

one_line_idea: Models trained on top-of-atmosphere reflectance partially learn the atmosphere: paired L1C/L2A evaluation of the same scenes will show atmospherically corrected training transfers better across dates and regions by a measurable margin.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Sentinel-2 distributes both top-of-atmosphere (L1C) and surface-reflectance (L2A) products of identical acquisitions; benchmark datasets are built inconsistently from either level, and models are compared without controlling for it.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Training on L1C couples model features to atmospheric state (aerosol, water vapor) that varies out-of-sample, so L2A-trained models will show smaller cross-date and cross-region degradation, and the difference will grow with atmospheric variability between train and test conditions, isolating the atmosphere as a learnable nuisance.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] L2A-trained models will lose at least 30% less accuracy than L1C-trained twins when transferred across seasons/regions with high atmospheric contrast, with the gap correlating with an atmospheric-distance measure (r >= 0.4); kill the idea if the transfer gap difference is under 10% relative or uncorrelated with atmospheric distance.
why_important: The field builds datasets from whichever product is convenient; a quantified atmosphere-learning effect would standardize dataset construction and explain part of cross-dataset irreproducibility.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Atmospheric correction is a preprocessing staple; measuring what models learn from residual atmosphere with paired same-scene products appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build paired L1C/L2A training sets of identical scenes and labels, train twins, and evaluate transfer across date/region splits stratified by atmospheric contrast from scene metadata.
main_risk: L2A correction itself has artifacts (correction failures over bright surfaces), which could penalize the corrected variant for processing reasons rather than physics.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Product level is treated as an interchangeable detail because networks are assumed to normalize away atmospheric effects.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Deep features may indeed be invariant to smooth atmospheric perturbations, making product level irrelevant beyond a fraction of a point.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: EuroSAT/BigEarthNet scenes re-downloaded at both processing levels with ResNet-50 and SatMAE; paired training runs in about 25 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$50).

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A large share of mountain-area classification error is deterministic illumination effect rather than genuine spectral ambiguity: physically correcting irradiance using DEM-derived incidence and shadow maps will recover a substantial fraction of the flat-vs-mountain accuracy gap, more than adding the DEM as a raw input channel, because the physical model imposes the correct functional form.

why_important: Mountain regions host critical monitoring targets (forests, glaciers, hazards); knowing whether their error is correctable optics or true ambiguity directs both preprocessing standards and sensor investment.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Topographic correction is a classical remote-sensing technique; its quantified value against modern deep models and the correction-vs-channel comparison appear unbenchmarked.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Stratify a public land-cover benchmark by terrain ruggedness, apply DEM-based irradiance correction versus DEM-as-channel versus raw, and compare accuracy gaps across strata.
main_risk: DEM resolution (30 m) may be too coarse for fine shadow boundaries, capping the correctable fraction for high-resolution imagery.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Terrain effects are assumed learnable from data diversity, making explicit physical correction obsolete legacy practice.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mountain error may be dominated by class confusion intrinsic to steep-terrain vegetation, not by illumination at all.

one_line_idea: Band-dropout training makes multispectral models band-set-invariant, enabling zero-shot transfer across sensors with different band configurations (Sentinel-2 to Landsat) at a small, quantified cost on the native sensor.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Earth-observation sensors differ in band count, centers, and widths; models are locked to one sensor's band stack, so every sensor needs its own model and archive-spanning analyses (Landsat era plus Sentinel era) are blocked.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Training with randomized band subsets plus band-identity encodings (center wavelength, bandwidth as metadata per channel) yields a single model that accepts any band configuration, and its zero-shot accuracy on an unseen sensor will approach sensor-specific training much closer than naive band-matching heuristics, because wavelength conditioning lets it interpolate spectral response.

why_important: A band-agnostic backbone would unify 50 years of multi-sensor archives for climate-scale analysis and free operational teams from per-sensor retraining, one of the field's most requested capabilities.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Wavelength-conditioned inputs appear in recent geospatial models; a pre-registered cross-sensor zero-shot fraction with band-dropout as the mechanism and hard kill thresholds appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train with band dropout and wavelength encodings on one sensor's public data, evaluate zero-shot on a second sensor's benchmark with harmonized labels, and compare against sensor-native and band-matched baselines.
main_risk: Radiometric calibration differences between sensors (beyond band definitions) may dominate, capping zero-shot transfer regardless of band handling.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Cross-sensor transfer is handled by resampling bands to a common subset, accepting the information loss as unavoidable.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Spectral response interpolation may fail for bands with no nearby training coverage (e.g., red-edge to none), making zero-shot brittle exactly where sensors differ most.

one_line_idea: Pan-sharpening hallucinates high-frequency chroma that shifts small-object detection in measurable ways, so detection pipelines consuming pan-sharpened products inherit fabrication errors invisible in image-quality metrics.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Commercial imagery is commonly delivered pan-sharpened: low-resolution multispectral fused with high-resolution panchromatic, a partially hallucinatory inverse problem; detection models are trained and run on these products as if they were measurements.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESis] Pan-sharpening errors are not neutral noise for detection: comparing detection on pan-sharpened inputs versus a dual-stream model consuming native panchromatic and multispectral separately will show the fused product both creates false positives at chroma-hallucination sites and misses objects whose spectral signature was averaged away, with a net measurable cost that grows for objects near the multispectral resolution limit.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Dual-stream native-resolution detection will beat pan-sharpened single-stream by at least 3 mAP points on small objects (under 3x multispectral GSD) while tying within 1 point on large objects; kill the idea if pan-sharpened input ties or wins on small objects, meaning hallucination is detection-neutral.
why_important: Operational feeds (defense, maritime, urgent response) are pan-sharpened by default at the provider level; if fusion hurts small-object detection, the standard delivery pipeline is destroying capability that native products retain.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Pan-sharpening quality is evaluated with image metrics; a detection-outcome audit of fusion hallucination with object-size stratification appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a public dataset providing native panchromatic and multispectral bands, train pan-sharpened-input and dual-stream detectors with matched capacity, and compare mAP stratified by object size relative to multispectral GSD.
main_risk: Dual-stream architectures introduce their own design choices; several fusion points must be tried to avoid attributing architecture effects to the input products.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Pan-sharpened products are treated as strictly superior inputs because they look sharper and score well on perceptual metrics.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detectors may be robust to chroma hallucination because they rely on panchromatic-derived edges, making fusion effects negligible.

one_line_idea: Optical biomass and canopy-height regressors hide a physical saturation ceiling: stratifying error by lidar-measured structure will show accuracy collapses beyond the spectral saturation point while global metrics look healthy, and SAR fusion lifts specifically that stratum.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Optical reflectance saturates with canopy density (leaf-area index beyond moderate values adds no optical signal), yet deep models regress biomass and canopy height from optical imagery and report aggregate errors dominated by abundant low-biomass areas.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Learned optical regressors achieve their headline numbers on the unsaturated regime and degrade to near-uninformative beyond saturation, exploiting texture and context to mask the failure; spaceborne lidar footprints provide the reference to expose the regime structure, and adding SAR (which penetrates canopy) will improve the saturated stratum specifically, confirming the mechanism.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Above the saturation stratum, optical-only correlation with lidar reference will fall below half its unsaturated value, and SAR fusion will recover at least 30% of the saturated-stratum deficit while adding under 10% in the unsaturated stratum; kill the idea if optical accuracy is regime-flat (ratio above 0.8) or SAR gains are uniform across regimes.
why_important: Forest carbon markets and climate policy consume these maps; regime-blind aggregate metrics overstate reliability exactly in high-carbon dense forests where the stakes are highest.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Spectral saturation is classical ecology-remote-sensing knowledge; a regime-stratified audit of modern deep regressors with a mechanism-confirming fusion test appears unassembled.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pair public lidar footprints with optical and SAR imagery, train optical-only and fusion regressors, and report error stratified by lidar-derived density regimes.
main_risk: Lidar footprint geolocation error and sparse sampling complicate stratified evaluation; footprint-level matching must be quality-filtered.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Deep models are presumed to circumvent spectral saturation via texture cues, an assumption rarely stress-tested against structural references.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Texture and context may genuinely carry high-biomass signal at fine GSD, keeping optical accuracy respectable beyond spectral saturation.

one_line_idea: Urbanization is nearly irreversible at monitoring timescales, and decoding land-cover time series under a monotonicity constraint removes temporal flicker while leaving accuracy unchanged, exploiting process physics that frame-independent models ignore.

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Enforcing class-transition monotonicity (urban absorbing state) as a decoding constraint over the time series will eliminate most flicker and slightly improve per-date accuracy near transition dates, because the constraint is true of the underlying process; the transition-date estimates will also sharpen, measured against high-confidence construction records.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Temporal smoothing is ubiquitous; framing irreversibility as a decodable absorbing-state constraint with transition-dating validation appears rare in the deep-learning era.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run per-date inference on a public dense-time-series benchmark, apply monotone dynamic-programming decoding on urban classes, and evaluate flicker, per-date accuracy, and transition-date error against labels.
main_risk: Demolition-to-greenfield does occur (rare); the constraint needs an escape probability or it will propagate rare errors forward indefinitely.
